newsitem.title: USA: USDA sees farm income dipping in 1997.
newsitem.headline: USDA sees farm income dipping in 1997.

text.p: The U.S. Department of Agriculture Monday forecast U.S. net farm income would dip to $40 billion in 1997 from the record $52 billion seen for 1996, sapped by lower grain prices.

In a quarterly report, USDA predicted grain prices would be lower in 1997 as world supplies increased, causing crop cash receipts to decline. It pegged 1997 crop receipts at $102 billion in 1997, down from $108 billion forecast for 1996.
Cash receipts for cattle were seen rising as ranchers reduce herds and lift prices, but a dip in dairy receipts will keep total livestock receipts close to 1996 levels, USDA said.

USDA said production expenses are forcast to climb to a record high of $184 billion in 1997, up from $183 billion seen for 1996. Production expenses have risen yearly since 1992. Seed, feeder livestock and fuel expenses are expected to post the largest percentage increases in 1997, USDA said.

Under the 1996 farm bill, direct government payments are forecast at $7.6 billion in 1997, down from the $7.8 billion forecast for 1996. During 1990-95, farmers got 5 percent of their cash income from direct government payments, which averaged about $9 billion a year, USDA said.
Smaller farms with under $250,000 in annual sales are seen facing the biggest decrease in net cash income in 1997 because they usually depend more on wheat and corn for income.
